summary.text: The sieve of Eratosthenes is an ancient algorithm for finding all prime numbers up to any given limit.
It marks the multiples of each prime as composite, starting with 2, and the numbers left unmarked at the end are the primes.
Unlike trial division, which tests each candidate, it generates the composites from their prime factors and gets the primes for free between them.

facts.label: Earliest known reference
facts.value: Nicomachus's Introduction to Arithmetic, early 2nd century CE

facts.label: Credited to
facts.value: Eratosthenes of Cyrene, a 3rd-century BCE Greek mathematician

facts.label: Key property
facts.value: Only additions are needed, no multiplications or divisions

facts.label: Main weakness
facts.value: Memory requirements, not the number of operations

items.prompt: In a sieve run, the number 15 gets crossed out twice. Why?

options.label: It is a multiple of both 3 and 5
It is a prime that was checked twice
It is a multiple of 2 and of 15
The sieve makes two passes over every number

items.explain: Some numbers are marked more than once; 15 is marked once for 3 and once for 5.

items.prompt: The sieve has crossed out the multiples of every prime it found. What do the untouched numbers left in the list represent?

options.label: The composite numbers
The odd numbers only
The primes
The numbers that were skipped by mistake

items.explain: Once all multiples of each discovered prime are marked as composite, the remaining unmarked numbers are primes.

items.prompt: After crossing out multiples of the smaller primes, the next uncrossed number you meet is always prime. Why?

options.label: It has more digits than the earlier primes
It was never tested, so nothing says otherwise
It is odd, and every odd number is prime
If it were composite, a smaller prime would already have crossed it out

items.explain: A composite number would have been marked as a multiple of some smaller prime.

items.prompt: What most clearly separates the sieve from checking each number with trial division?

options.label: The sieve builds composites from primes, while trial division tests each candidate
The sieve tests every candidate against every smaller number
The sieve only works on odd numbers
Trial division never needs any prime numbers at all

items.explain: The sieve directly generates composites as multiples of primes instead of testing for them, getting the primes between the composites.

items.prompt: Someone runs the sieve on an enormous range and it struggles. According to the note by Sorenson, what is the usual problem?

options.label: Too many multiplications to carry out
Memory requirements rather than the number of operations
Primes become impossible to recognize
The multiples drift out of order

items.explain: The problem is not the number of operations but the memory needed, since the range may not fit in memory and cache use is poor.

items.prompt: Once a new prime is found, how are its multiples lined up for crossing out?

options.label: Evenly spaced, with a gap equal to that prime
Spaced by one more each time
Spaced by the number of primes found so far
Randomly across the list

items.explain: The multiples form a sequence starting from the prime with a constant difference equal to that prime.
